title: D&D: Mystic Horizon, Chapter 1 Episode 1: Killing Zombozos

excerpt.verification: The whole recording is the excerpt, because duration is the property being tested. Measured from the media rather than read from the description: ffprobe reports 14238.058231 s (3 h 57 m 18 s) over the audio stream obtained as yt-dlp format 140 (AAC-LC, 44.1 kHz, 128 kbit/s), 230265075 bytes, SHA-256 83999e0cb827ac2243bdc097b5097c2e990b9cf5a00c4e02f31e0332cd20af7f on 2026-07-26. That digest stays in prose and is deliberately not recorded as source.media_sha256, because media_sha256 asserts something this source cannot support: the platform re-encodes and serves signed, expiring URLs, so a second downloader's bytes will differ and the scripts/fetch_benchmark_media.py comparison has nothing to compare. It is a record of what one acquisition returned. What does establish identity here is source.content_fingerprint - a loudness envelope of the decoded audio, which survives re-encoding - and every anchor below is an offset into the recording it identifies rather than into any particular file. Before using an anchor against a copy you obtained yourself, run `uv run python scripts/audio_identity.py verify <your-copy> --against benchmarks/fingerprints/mystic-horizon-ch1ep1-killing-zombozos.json` and apply any offset it reports. The procedure, its demonstration across three encodings and two negative controls, and the two ways it was wrong first are in benchmarks/notes/recording-identity.md. Acquire with `yt-dlp -f 140`, and expect to re-derive the recording rather than the bytes.

recording_conditions.observations: Measured from the acquired audio: nominally stereo but effectively one mixed track (L-R residual -55.2 dB against -20.7 dB programme, 34 dB down), so there is no per-speaker channel to diarize from. Delivered at 44.1 kHz with a hard AAC ceiling near 15.4 kHz; energy above 12 kHz sits 26 dB down. Integrated loudness -14.6 LUFS with a 17.1 LU range and a true peak of +0.7 dBFS - clipping, and a dynamic range more than twice the Hiddengrid item's 8.2 LU, which is the unpolished-audio property this candidate was admitted for. 3285 gaps longer than 0.5 s at -40 dB across the recording, about 14 per minute, indicating dense turn-taking rather than monologue. Fourteen per cent of the timeline produces no transcript segment, and none of it is silence: silencedetect at -40 dB with a 1.5 s minimum finds no silent run anywhere in 3 h 57 m, while the same detector at a 0.5 s minimum finds 3285. So the recording is gapped at the scale of a breath and never quiet at the scale of a pause. That the uncovered time carries no speech rather than dropped speech was checked with a second engine over the worst-covered five minutes (00:39:00-00:44:00): large-v3-turbo covers 76.3% of it and medium.en 72.3%, the second engine covering less rather than more, and the 19 seconds it adds contain the words 'I', 'You' and 'Um'. Two independent engines agree the gap is laughter, dice, breath and room. About 34 minutes of the file is uncovered - 14.2% of 14239 seconds - of which 694 stretches run longer than two seconds; those are two measurements, one counting seconds and one counting runs, not the same figure twice. That is what a cost measured against wall-clock duration will be paying for. Speaker count is now read from the audio rather than from the credit line, and the two disagree in both directions. The description names WOLFVAME as game master with Sir Horse, ReaperSect, Lizzie and Sammy Stuffies as players; the audio establishes in its first twenty seconds that Lizzie's character Opal is absent, and it carries a participant called Yucky, twenty times over three hours, who is in no credit line. Five is therefore the count of speaking roles the recording itself presents - the game master, Honse, Wrugmil, Scarlet and Yucky - and it happens to coincide with the credited five while naming a different set. proven_distinct_speakers stays null, and not for want of effort. Nobody has listened, so no pairwise distinctness was established by ear; and the other route, running a diarizer, would put a provider in truth.contaminating_providers for the one item best placed to measure diarization at length. Buying one field at that price is a bad trade and would be invisible once the number was written down. music_or_effects is null because the question was sampled, not answered: no music was found in five windows totalling about ten minutes (0-4 min, and 90 s each at 1 h, 2 h, 3 h and 3 h 55 m) out of a 3 h 57 m file, and the three annotated windows added nine minutes without finding any. false would still claim a complete inspection nobody performed. The players are remote rather than round one table, which is why this does not fill the single-room tier - but that is inference, not a source statement. What the description actually carries is a Discord invite link and a cast credited by handle; it nowhere says the session was played over Discord. The inference points in the conservative direction, since it keeps the single-room tier empty rather than claiming to fill it, and listening would settle it. The commands behind the acoustic figures, and their raw output, are committed in benchmarks/notes/b03-candidate-measurements.md; the coverage, silence and speaker figures added at B04 are in benchmarks/notes/mystic-horizon-ch1ep1-annotation.md, and every per-second level they rest on can be re-derived from the committed content fingerprint without the audio.

important_entities.label: Yucky
important_entities.evidence: Both engines carry the name at 00:01:55, addressed directly by the game master - 'so yucky what's up, what's the word of the day' - and again at 00:09:37, 00:36:42 and 03:03:50, where the game master calls it twice waiting for an answer. Twenty occurrences across 3 h 02 m, always addressing a participant, always in the third person masculine when discussed. This is the one label here with no written source behind it, exactly as Freya is on the Hiddengrid item: the publisher's description credits five people by handle and gives each a character, and Yucky is none of them. So the audio establishes that a participant is called this and roughly how it sounds; nothing establishes how it is written, nor whether it is a nickname for one of the credited five or a sixth person the credits omit. Both readings fit what is audible. A scoring run that penalises a variant spelling here is measuring a question this item cannot pose, and one that resolves it to a credited name is guessing.

important_entities.label: Reaper
important_entities.evidence: Both engines at 00:02:42, one player addressing another by name - 'I wouldn't know any of this, Reaper, I'm vegetarian' - and both again at 03:53:44, 3 h 51 m later, when the game master tells him to name the weapon he has just created. This is a person and not a character: the description credits the handle ReaperSect, playing Wrugmil, and the audio uses the short form throughout. The pair is the corpus's clearest person-against-character case at length, because both names are spoken for the same human being hours apart.

important_entities.label: Honse
important_entities.evidence: Both engines carry the name at 00:09:23 when the game master turns to him, and both again at 03:48:54 - 'you good, Hans?' - after he has gone quiet mid-scene. Thirty-five occurrences in between. Both engines write it 'Hans' and neither could do otherwise, because that is what it sounds like; the spelling 'Honse' comes from the publisher's description, which credits 'Sir Horse (Honse, Fighter)' and makes it a pun on the player's own handle that no listener would recover. The audio establishes the name is spoken and how; the description establishes how it is written. Neither source does the other's work, which is the distinction this field exists to keep.

important_entities.label: souls
important_entities.evidence: Both engines at 00:09:32, 'five days for 15 souls, just an FYI', the game master keeping a running tally out loud. Souls are this campaign's currency and its central homebrew mechanic - counted, spent, fed to a weapon, and warned about ('if you have 100 souls, you will lose all of them' at 02:24:24). Ninety-eight occurrences across 3 h 42 m. It is an item rather than a quest because the table treats it as a resource with a balance, and the balance is stated as a number twice, at 00:17:09 and 03:30:03.

important_entities.label: Scarlet
important_entities.evidence: Both engines at 00:36:37, the game master addressing the character during a scouting turn, and both again at 03:17:28 in the callback that closes her arc. The primary writes 'scarlet' and the secondary 'Scarlett', a split neither can settle; the publisher's description credits 'Sammy Stuffies (Scarlet, Druid)' and settles it in writing. She is also the case where person and character come apart in the audio itself: the character is Scarlet, the player is Sammy, and the session's closing recap at 03:51:37 says 'Sammy did die' about the character's death.

important_entities.label: Wrugmil
important_entities.evidence: Both engines produce a two-syllable name in the same exchange at 00:36:37-00:36:44 and neither produces the same string: the primary writes 'rug mill' twice, the secondary 'rug me' then 'rug meal'. What is established from audio is that a name of that shape is spoken and that it belongs to a character distinct from Yucky, since the game master corrects himself between the two in one breath. The spelling is the publisher's - 'ReaperSect (Wrugmil, Bard/Rogue)' - and no decoder came close to it. Recorded as an example of the failure mode fantasy names produce: two engines, one sound, two wrong strings, and a written source doing all the orthographic work.

important_entities.label: Opal
important_entities.evidence: Both engines at 00:00:19: 'so Opal is technically AFK, she said she'll catch up with you guys'. The character is written into the fiction as travelling with the party while her player is away, and the arrangement is referred to again at 00:26:19 and 01:19:43. This is the item's trap for entity extraction: Opal is a real party member, established by name in the first twenty seconds, and she does almost nothing for four hours. A system that reports her as a participant is right; one that reports her actions is inventing them.

important_entities.label: the hand axe
important_entities.evidence: Both engines at 03:17:28, in the same sentence in which its earlier use is recalled: 'you saw what the hand axe did with Scarlet, right, when I revived her'. The exchange continues past the anchor with 'that axe hurt you when you use it' and 'as long as I don't use it to attack I'll be okay', both engines. Thirty occurrences from 00:15:56 onward, including the throw at 00:19:55. The weapon costs its wielder to use and is fed with souls, which is why it and the currency are separate targets rather than one.

important_entities.label: the black soul eater
important_entities.evidence: Both engines at 02:07:44, 'for my action I'm gonna throw black soul eater, I'm using the extended range one', and both again at 02:08:14 when the throw is resolved. First mentioned at 00:03:10 and last at 03:34:45. A second named weapon, distinct from the hand axe, thrown at range while the party is losing a fight - the moment that most tests whether a system keeps two similar magical items apart across four hours.

important_events.label: The session opens with one credited player absent, and her character written into the fiction as travelling with the party anyway.
important_events.evidence: Both engines at 00:00:19-00:00:51. The game master explains the absence in table terms and in fiction terms in the same breath - 'she's going home, she's confused', 'she's with you guys but she's kind of like sleeping' - and the table jokes over it. Twelve seconds in, before any play, and it governs four hours: a system that misses it will attribute the party's decisions to five people.

important_events.label: The first action of the session is butchering a deer killed before the recording started.
important_events.evidence: Both engines at 00:01:09 and through to 00:04:16: the kill is prior ('I'm pretty sure it's already dead'), a survival check is called for the butchering, and the yield is negotiated in days of food. The hide is picked up at 00:09:37 and its refinement into armour discussed at 00:10:02. The kill itself happened off-recording, so a chronicle that reports the party killing a deer in this session has invented the event that the audio explicitly places before it.

important_events.label: The soul economy is introduced with a running tally kept aloud by the game master.
important_events.evidence: Both engines at 00:09:32. The tally is restated at 00:17:09 ('15 souls in total') and the mechanic elaborated at 00:16:47 and 00:17:17, where souls are described as feeding the axe. This is the opening of the thread the session closes on, and the number stated here is what makes the closing number legible as an outcome rather than a fact.

important_events.label: A player's phone call interrupts a scene mid-action, the table follows the anecdote for half a minute, and the game master pulls it back.
important_events.evidence: Both engines from 00:42:15 to 00:42:52. A player's brother rings twice about a missing portion of chicken, is hung up on, then telephones the player's girlfriend to complain; the game master says 'okay, let's actually get back to the session, hopefully' and re-asks the question he had asked before the interruption. None of it is campaign content and all of it is inside a scene, mid-stealth-check, with no edit or pause marking it. This window was chosen on acoustic measurement alone, before anyone knew what was in it, which is why the passage counts as a test rather than as a selected example.

important_events.label: The party leader's character dies in the zombie fight, and the table starts looking up how to bring her back.
important_events.evidence: Both engines at 02:06:49-02:06:52, 'wait, are you actually dead dead' answered with 'he's dead'; the primary alone adds 'we lost our leader', which the secondary drops, so that phrase is single-engine and the death itself is not. The player then states the route out at 02:08:38, both engines: 'there is a way to get me back, you guys have to have a resurrection spell'. Raise dead through a town priest is discussed at 02:09:41 and the time limit on a soul at 02:09:51. The pronouns in this passage are worth noting rather than smoothing: the character is Scarlet and the table says 'he' throughout, so a system that infers character gender from the audio here will get it wrong.

important_events.label: The revival is recalled two hours after the death, and used to explain what the hand axe costs its wielder.
important_events.evidence: Both engines at 03:17:26-03:17:41: 'it's tough to explain, but you saw what the hand axe did with Scarlet, right, when I revived her' - then 'it took some of my strength and I'm using the axe to gain back my strength', answered with 'but that axe hurt you when you use it'. The revival is not narrated when it happens; it is established here, retrospectively, 1 h 10 m later, in a conversation between two characters about something else. This is the anchor that makes the item worth its length: nothing in a ten-minute excerpt can pose it.

important_events.label: The soul count reaches a hundred and the game master narrates the consequence he had set up hours earlier.
important_events.evidence: Both engines at 03:29:51-03:29:56: 'you feel this humongous burst of energy and power dwelling deep inside you, as you did not just consume one, not two, not even ten - a hundred souls'. The balance is then stated as 91 at 03:30:03, both engines, after a deduction the player narrates. The threshold matters because the game master warned at 02:24:24 that a hundred souls would be lost all at once, and offers a question answered instead at 03:37:29. Souls are also collected here from an ant colony, whose size the player has looked up mid-session.

important_events.label: The session closes with the table's own recap of what happened, in three clauses.
important_events.evidence: Both engines at 03:51:34-03:51:39: 'we almost died to zombies', 'Sammy did die', 'we got a hundred souls'. The publisher's own summary of the session, spoken by a player, 3 h 51 m in - and a direct target for any system that produces a summary of this recording. Note the second clause names the person rather than the character who died, unprompted, which is how this table actually refers to the event.

threads.label: The soul economy, from a running tally of fifteen to the hundred that closes the session
threads.evidence: 3 h 42 m 02 s. Opens at 00:09:32 with the game master counting souls aloud - 'five days for 15 souls' - and closes at 03:51:39 with a player's recap clause, 'we got a hundred souls'. It is one thread and not two mentions of a word: the hundred is a threshold the game master set at 02:24:24, the count is stated as a number at both ends, and the closing clause is offered as the session's outcome. Every anchor in it is carried by both engines.

threads.label: Scarlet dies, is revived off-narration, and the revival is explained an hour later to account for what the axe costs
threads.evidence: 2 h 40 m 51 s. Opens at 00:36:37 with the character addressed by name during a scouting turn, runs through her death at 02:06:52 and the resurrection discussion at 02:08:38, and closes at 03:17:28 with 'you saw what the hand axe did with Scarlet, right, when I revived her'. The revival itself is never narrated; the last anchor is the only place the recording states it happened, and it states it in passing, in a conversation about a weapon. A system that has dropped the death cannot make sense of the closing exchange at all.

threads.label: Reaper, a player addressed by name in the third minute and in the last
threads.evidence: 3 h 48 m 52 s between the first anchor at 00:02:42 and the recap at 03:51:34, and 3 h 51 m 02 s to his last named appearance at 03:53:44, which is outside the last target's anchor and so is not what is claimed here. The thread is participant continuity rather than plot: the same human being is addressed by the same short form at both ends, while his character is addressed by a different name in between. It is the cheapest test in the item and the one most likely to fail quietly, since nothing about it is dramatic enough to survive summarisation.

truth.method: Machine-assisted, 2026-07-26, not a human ear. The full 3 h 57 m 18 s was decoded once by whisper.cpp large-v3-turbo at beam 5 on Metal, and every span carrying a claimed anchor was decoded again by openai-whisper medium.en - a different implementation and a different model family - over an independent 70-second clip cut from the same private copy, so the second reading is not a re-run of the first. Both ran locally; nothing was sent anywhere. A target is verified only where both engines carry it at the same moment, and where they diverge the divergence is written into the evidence rather than resolved by preference: 'we lost our leader' is marked single-engine, and Wrugmil's three different spellings are all quoted. Structure was measured with ffmpeg rather than inferred from any model - per-second RMS from the committed content fingerprint, silence detection, and ASR coverage per block - and the annotation windows were chosen from those measurements before anyone knew what the windows contained. Spelling is treated as a separate question from sound throughout. Honse, Wrugmil and Scarlet take their orthography from the publisher's video description, which credits each player with a character; the audio establishes only that a name of that sound is spoken, and each item says which source did which. Yucky has no written source at all. The three window transcripts under benchmarks/transcripts/ are drafts from the same two engines and are not a reference: no person has corrected them, they declare that in their own status field, and a word error rate computed against them measures agreement with large-v3-turbo. benchmarks/notes/mystic-horizon-ch1ep1-annotation.md records the decoding, the window selection and the limits; benchmarks/notes/recording-identity.md records how a reader establishes that their copy is the recording these anchors are offsets into.
truth.notes: Nothing here was heard by a person. Every target is audio_machine_assisted and there are no audio_observed targets in this item at all, which is the honest state and not a placeholder: the annotator has no ears. Both engines are in contaminating_providers and neither can be scored against these targets without declaring the dependency. What the two-engine rule buys is narrower than it looks - it catches one engine inventing a word, and it does not catch both engines mishearing the same way, which they demonstrably do, since large-v3-turbo and medium.en share a lineage. Wrugmil is the standing example: two engines, one sound, two wrong strings. Three names here take their spelling from the publisher's description and not from any decode - Honse, Wrugmil and Scarlet - and each item says so. Yucky takes its spelling from nowhere: it is not in the credits, and the corpus does not know whether it names a sixth participant or nicknames one of the five. The description was used only to settle orthography and never to establish that something is in the recording; every target above is anchored to a moment both engines carry, and an item that could have been written from the description would not be acceptance evidence for this goal. A negative control worth stating: the description credits Lizzie playing Opal, and the audio establishes in its first twenty seconds that she is absent. Any account of this session that has her acting is drawing on the credits rather than on the recording. benchmarks/notes/mystic-horizon-ch1ep1-annotation.md carries the window selection, the structural measurements, and what a score here does and does not diagnose.

rights.copyright_holder: SIR HORSE and the credited participants; Dungeons & Dragons material remains with Wizards of the Coast
rights.license: Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 (YouTube's 'Creative Commons - reuse allowed' setting)
rights.review_notes: Read from the watch page's own markup on 2026-07-26, which carries the 'Creative Commons (reuse allowed)' licence row; yt-dlp independently reports license='Creative Commons Attribution license (reuse allowed)' for this video id. The detection was controlled: the same check finds no such row on any of the six candidates supplied with the goal, and does find it on other videos, so the absence elsewhere is a real difference rather than a broken test. Three limits are recorded rather than smoothed over. First, the uploader can only license what the uploader owns; the campaign is described as mostly homebrew, but the system and any published material remain Wizards of the Coast's, exactly as Shadowrun remains Topps' in the Hiddengrid item. Second, CC BY permits redistribution with attribution, but redistribution stays restricted here on repository policy - media and full transcripts do not enter Git under any licence. Third, the content licence is what grants reuse; obtaining the file from a platform is separately subject to that platform's terms, which is a question about the acquisition route rather than about this licence.

selection.diagnostic_value: The corpus's only long-form scoreable item, at the product's real target duration: 3 h 57 m in one continuous live stream with no chapter break, re-setup or edit concealing a discontinuity. What it can pose that no other item can is thread survival. Three threads are recorded with both ends anchored to moments two engines agree on, the longest running 3 h 42 m, and one of them turns on a revival that is never narrated when it happens and is established only in passing an hour later - so a system that dropped the death cannot make sense of the exchange that closes it. Around that sit an entity established in the first twenty seconds who then does almost nothing for four hours, a currency counted aloud at both ends of the session, two similar magical weapons that have to stay apart, a person-against-character split spoken both ways for the same human being hours apart, and half a minute of a player's phone call about chicken sitting inside a stealth check with nothing marking it as out of fiction. It also probes what length does to cost: 14% of the timeline carries no transcribable speech and none of it is silence, so throughput measured against wall-clock will differ sharply from throughput measured against speech. Its 17.1 LU range and clipped peaks additionally probe unpolished level handling, which the corpus's other amateur item does not, having been levelled to 8.2 LU in post.
risks: Nothing here was heard by a person. The truth is two engines agreeing, which catches one of them inventing a word and does not catch both mishearing the same way - and they share a lineage, so they do. Wrugmil is the standing example. A human correction pass on the windows is prepared and not done: benchmarks/transcripts/mystic-horizon-ch1ep1-killing-zombozos/correction-worksheet.md.

Nine minutes of 237 are transcribed. The entity, event and thread layer spans the whole recording, but everything between the anchors is unannotated, so a score here is evidence about the anchors and about coherence across them, not about the four hours as a body of text.

The window transcripts are drafts and will be read as a reference by someone. They declare usable_for_word_error_rate false in their own JSON so a program can refuse them, but the failure mode is a person, not a program.

One committed window reproduces private conversation. W2 carries about 35 s of a player's phone call about a family argument, out of fiction, which is exactly why the window is diagnostic - but it is the only place committed text in this repository reproduces something private. No third party is named and the publisher livestreamed and licensed it himself, so this is a re-publication of public material rather than a disclosure. The window was chosen on acoustic measurement before its content was known, so nobody decided to include it. Whether the repository wants verbatim text of this kind is a policy question above this goal and is open; benchmarks/transcripts/README.md states the position rather than assuming one. If the source is taken down this text should go with it.

Bytes are not reproducible: YouTube re-encodes and serves expiring URLs. Identity is established instead by source.content_fingerprint, demonstrated in benchmarks/notes/recording-identity.md, which recovers the offset to within about 33 ms. That is far finer than any anchor here needs and it is a floor, not zero. A disappeared video is recognisable from the recorded id, channel id, title, duration and fingerprint.

Remote play mixed to one track, so it does not fill the single-room single-microphone tier, which stays empty. That the players are remote is inferred from the handles and the invite link in the description, not stated by the publisher.
A 941-subscriber channel with 79 views on this video may take the recording down without notice, and there is no archival copy the project may republish.
